query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting Ta with Nb in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy reduces the overall density while preserving its high strength and phase stability at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of roughly 10.21 g/cm³ and excellent mechanical performance at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace Ta with an equivalent atomic fraction of Nb to form HfMoNbTiZr.
generation.conditions: Mechanical characterization (tensile and/or compressive tests) conducted in the as-cast state at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase BCC solid-solution structure through substitutional alloying, because Nb and Ta have similar atomic sizes and crystallographic preferences.
generation.mechanism: Replacing the heavy Ta (density ~16.65 g/cm³) with lighter Nb (density ~8.57 g/cm³) reduces the overall density of the alloy while maintaining the lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening responsible for high mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HfMoNbTiZr alloy is expected to show a density reduction on the order of 10–15% relative to HfMoTaTiZr, with yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility at room temperature and about 1000 °C remaining comparable (within roughly 10–15% variation).
generation.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy, known for its high strength and density of ~10.21 g/cm³.
generation.boundary: Applies to alloys synthesized via similar as-cast processing routes, with performance verified under standard mechanical loading conditions at room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of density reduction and retention of mechanical properties may vary; further experimental validation is needed to confirm the balance between reduced density and maintained strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the HfMoNbTiZr alloy under identical as-cast conditions as HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize the phase structure (using XRD and SEM), measure the density (via Archimedes method), and perform tensile (and/or compressive) tests at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
measurements: Mechanical tests (yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility) at RT and ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy does not exhibit at least a ~10% reduction in density or if its mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength or ductility) degrade by more than approximately 10–15% compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, the hypothesis will be rejected.

Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Several theoretical models of solid-solution strengthening have been proposed to explain how different constituent elements affect room-temperature or elevated-temperature strength [,]. We previously designed a RHEA that exhibited higher elevated-temperature strength and discussed the effect of the constituent elements on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys by using the subtraction method []. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add elements such as Mo, which significantly interact with the other elements. For higher elevated-temperature strength, one should add the elements that possess a high melting point such as Mo, Nb, or Ta. For higher ductility, one should add more Nb. With Ti or Zr addition, both the elevated-temperature strength and the density decrease.

drafts.hypothesis: Substituting Ta with Nb in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower the overall density while retaining the high strength and phase stability at both room temperature and at roughly 1000 °C.
drafts.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³, exhibiting excellent mechanical performance at room and elevated temperatures due in part to a single-phase, substitutionally hardened structure.
drafts.intervention: Replace the Ta component with an equivalent atomic fraction of Nb, leading to a new composition HfMoNbTiZr.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical property and phase stability evaluations under standard tensile loading at room temperature and at elevated temperature (approximately 1000 °C).
drafts.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase BCC (or closely related) structure maintained by the substitutional solid-solution effect, as Nb’s atomic size and crystal structure are similar to those of Ta.
drafts.mechanism: Nb has a significantly lower density than Ta and, owing to similar atomic radii and BCC structure, it can substitute without inducing detrimental lattice distortions. This preserves the high-temperature phase stability and mechanical strength while reducing the overall alloy density.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The alloy HfMoNbTiZr is expected to show a lower density compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr while maintaining comparable yield and ultimate strengths at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
drafts.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with high mechanical performance and a density of ~10.21 g/cm³.
drafts.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C under tensile load conditions similar to the original testing protocols.

Characterize phase composition using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and measure density. Conduct standardized tensile tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C, including any relevant creep tests.
measurements: XRD for phase identification and lattice parameter analysis
Tensile testing for yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility at room temperature
Tensile testing at ~1000 °C for comparison of high-temperature mechanical properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy exhibits a significant decrease in mechanical properties (e.g., a drop in yield or ultimate strength by more than roughly 10%) or develops secondary phases or instabilities at ~1000 °C compared to the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy, the hypothesis will be rejected.

drafts.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy Ta component with a lighter refractory element like Nb in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce the overall density without sacrificing the alloy’s high strength at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
drafts.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g cm−3 and high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures.
drafts.intervention: Substitute Ta with Nb to form a novel HfMoNbTiZr alloy.
drafts.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (up to roughly 1000 °C) under mechanical loading representative of the original application conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Similar solid‐solution formation and lattice distortion effects are expected due to comparable atomic radii and bonding characteristics between Ta and Nb, preserving the microstructure responsible for high strength.
drafts.mechanism: Replacing Ta (density ~16.65 g cm−3) with Nb (density ~8.57 g cm−3) is anticipated to lower the alloy’s overall density. Since Nb is also a refractory element with a high melting point (around 2477 °C) and comparable strengthening behavior, it should maintain the high-temperature mechanical properties while reducing mass.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The alloy’s density is predicted to decrease by an estimated 10–15% relative to the original alloy, with mechanical properties (strength at room temperature and ~1000 °C) remaining comparable to those of the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
drafts.baseline: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with known high strength and density of ~10.21 g cm−3.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to alloys produced using similar casting conditions and processing routes, and the performance should be validated in the temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C under typical mechanical loading scenarios.

Characterize the as-cast microstructure using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Measure the alloy’s density and perform tensile or compressive mechanical tests at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C. Compare these results to the corresponding properties of the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
measurements: Density using Archimedes method or similar.
Room temperature tensile or compressive strength.
High temperature (≈1000 °C) tensile or compressive strength.
Phase structure analysis via XRD and SEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy does not exhibit a significant reduction in density relative to the original alloy, or if its mechanical properties at room temperature or ~1000 °C are significantly degraded (e.g., lower yield strength, loss of phase stability) compared to HfMoTaTiZr, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Partial substitution of high-density hafnium (Hf) with a lighter element such as scandium (Sc) in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce overall alloy density while retaining the excellent room‐temperature and ~1000°C mechanical properties.
drafts.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr exhibiting high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures with a density of about 10.21 g/cm³.
drafts.intervention: Replace a portion of Hf (e.g., 30–50%) with Sc to form a modified alloy composition, for example Hf(1–x)Sc(x)MoTaTiZr.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical testing under standard tensile and compressive loading conditions at room temperature and at approximately 1000°C.
drafts.structural_mediator: Retention of the single-phase (e.g., BCC) solid-solution structure via isomorphous substitution, as Sc can occupy similar lattice sites without disturbing the lattice significantly.
drafts.mechanism: Scandium has a lower atomic mass and density than hafnium. Its incorporation is expected to reduce the overall density while maintaining the lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening mechanisms that are critical for high strength at both room and elevated temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a lower density relative to the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr while preserving comparable yield and ultimate strengths at both room temperature and near 1000°C; the ductility should also remain within acceptable ranges.
drafts.baseline: The as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and demonstrated high strength over the temperature range of interest.
drafts.boundary: The performance is expected to be maintained under tensile and compressive loadings at room temperature and up to approximately 1000°C; effects outside these temperature/strain rate ranges are not addressed in this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with varying levels of Sc substitution for Hf (e.g., 0%, 30%, and 50%) while keeping the other elements constant. Use X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify that the single-phase BCC solid-solution structure is maintained. Then, measure density and perform standardized tensile and compressive tests at room temperature and ~1000°C.
measurements: Phase analysis using XRD and microstructure observation via SEM/TEM
Mechanical tests to record yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility at room temperature and 1000°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sc-substituted alloys do not show a significant reduction in density or if their yield strength, ultimate strength, or ductility at room temperature and ~1000°C are significantly lower than those of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if unwanted secondary phases form, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy Ta component with a lighter refractory element Nb (i.e. converting HfMoTaTiZr to HfMoNbTiZr) will reduce the overall density significantly while preserving the high room‐temperature and elevated-temperature (≈1000 °C) mechanical properties.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm3 and excellent strength at both room temperature and 1000 °C.
drafts.intervention: Substitute Ta (atomic mass ≈181) with Nb (atomic mass ≈93) to form the HfMoNbTiZr alloy.
drafts.conditions: Tests conducted in as-cast condition under standard tensile and compressive loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C.
drafts.structural_mediator: A single-phase BCC solid-solution microstructure achieved by substitutional alloying, which preserves the lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening mechanisms.
drafts.mechanism: By replacing the high-density Ta with lighter Nb while maintaining similar chemical interactions, the alloy’s average atomic mass drops. Nb also contributes to high melting temperatures and ductility. Thus, the density is lowered without a significant loss in the strength and plasticity that arise from solid-solution strengthening and the retention of a stable BCC structure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The HfMoNbTiZr alloy will exhibit a notably lower density compared to HfMoTaTiZr (targeting at least a 10%–15% reduction) while its yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C will remain similar (within about 10–15% of the original values).
drafts.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr showing high strength at RT and elevated temperatures but with a relatively high density (≈10.21 g/cm3).
drafts.boundary: Performance is evaluated under as-cast conditions with mechanical testing performed from room temperature up to 1000 °C under quasi-static (tensile/compressive) loading.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the HfMoNbTiZr alloy using the same as-cast processing as HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize its density (e.g., via Archimedes method), confirm phase stability with XRD and microstructural uniformity with SEM, and perform standard tensile and compressive tests at room temperature as well as at approximately 1000 °C.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate strength (tensile/compressive tests) at RT and ≈1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the substitution of Ta with Nb does not lead to a significant reduction in density (i.e., less than ~10% decrease) or if the mechanical properties (strength and ductility) at room temperature or around 1000 °C are degraded by more than about 10–15% relative to HfMoTaTiZr, the hypothesis will be rejected.
